- If sentiment is consistently low (≤0.2) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce forecast slope to avoid over-optimism.  
- If sentiment is high (≥0.5) and forecast is flat or declining, increase forecast slightly to capture bullish momentum.  
- After a sharp price spike, model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast slope in next 3–5 days to avoid overshoot.  
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive drops from peak), model often fails to adjust — apply downward bias correction.  
- If history shows volatility clustering (e.g., 3+ consecutive swings), forecast should be more volatile — avoid smooth linear trends.  
- For long horizons (e.g., 30d), model often underestimates late-period spikes — increase forecast tail (last 5–7 days) by 2–5% if sentiment is positive.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 values, model tends to be overly conservative — add small upward bias (e.g., +0.5–1.5%) to forecast.  
- When true outcome diverges sharply from history (e.g., >10% drop from recent peak), model often ignores it — adjust forecast to reflect recent volatility.
